title: Some sixteenth-century Roman theologians kept the view: Alfonso de Castro and Joseph Angles
source_text: XXI. Imo sententiam istam superiori saeculo in Schola Rom. retinuerunt adhuc Theologi nonnulli. Ut Alfonsus de Castro ordinis Minorum lib. de haeresibus in verbo Libertas. Est, inquit, adhuc Alia libertas quae opponitur necessitati, vel ut verius dicam coactioni. Et subjungit, quando dicimus hominis arbitrium esse liberum, istud intelligi de hac libertate. Alfonsi vero verba postea adoptavit & sua fecit Joseph Angles, designatus Episcopus Bosanensis, ex ordine quoque Minorum, in secundum librum sententiarum scribens. Nam postquam loquutus est de libertate gratiae & libertate gloriae, Tertio, inquit, est libertas, quae opponitur necessitati, vel, ut verius dicam, coactioni. Et haec est libertas naturae, de qua loquimur in praesentia. Et postea, ubi distinxit triplicem libertatem, Unam a coactione, Alteram a peccato, Tertiam a miseria, haec est illius Conclusio, Quoad libertatem primo modo, aeque in homine & in Angelo est liberum Arbitrium: Et ratio est, quia neque mali Angeli, neque boni, neque mali hominis voluntas cogi potest. In sequentibus vero postquam proposuit quaestionem illam, Utrum Actus liberi Arbitrii sit contingentium tantum, vel etiam necessariorum, Observat ex Bonaventura, liberum arbitrium posse dupliciter considerari, vel quatenus liberum est, vel quatenus deliberans est. Deinde subjungit duas conclusiones. 1. Actus liberi arbitrii potest esse, & est necessariorum. Ratio est, quia in Deo, angelis & in hominibus beatis, est liberum arbitrium, quod quidem immutabiliter, & necessario in suum actum exit; quia Deus per naturam, & Angelus & homo beatus per gloriam, immutabilis est. II. Si liberum Arbitrium secundo modo accipiatur, actus illius contingentium est. Ratio est, quia non consiliamur, neque consultamus de necessariis, & impossibilibus, sed de contingentibus, quae facere vel non facere in nostra potestate situm est. Ad distinctionem 24. & 25. quaest. unica de Libero Arbitrio art. 1. 2. & 3.
pass_a_gloss: Nay this opinion was still retained in the last century in the Roman School by some Theologians. As Alfonso de Castro of the order of Minors in his book on heresies under the word Liberty. There is, he says, besides Another liberty which is opposed to necessity, or to speak more truly to compulsion. And he adds that when we say man's choice is free, this is understood of this liberty. The words of Alfonso were afterward adopted and made his own by Joseph Angles, designated Bishop of Bosa, also of the order of Minors, writing on the second book of the sentences. For after he has spoken of the liberty of grace and the liberty of glory, Thirdly, he says, there is the liberty which is opposed to necessity, or, to speak more truly, to compulsion. And this is the liberty of nature, of which we speak at present. And afterward, where he distinguished a threefold liberty, One from compulsion, Another from sin, a Third from misery, this is his Conclusion, As to liberty in the first mode, free Choice is equally in man and in Angel: And the reason is, because neither the will of bad Angels, nor of good, nor of bad men can be compelled. But in what follows, after he proposed that question, Whether the Act of free Choice be of contingent things only, or also of necessary ones, He observes from Bonaventure, that free choice can be considered in two ways, either so far as it is free, or so far as it is deliberating. Then he adds two conclusions. 1. The act of free choice can be, and is, of necessary things. The reason is, because in God, angels and in blessed men, there is free choice, which indeed immutably, and necessarily goes forth into its act; because God by nature, and Angel and blessed man by glory, is immutable. II. If free Choice be taken in the second mode, its act is of contingent things. The reason is, because we do not take counsel, nor consult, about things necessary, and impossible, but about contingent things, which it lies in our power to do or not to do. On distinction 24. and 25. the single quest. on Free Choice art. 1. 2. and 3.
pass_b_english: Even in the last century some theologians of the Roman School still held this view. Alfonso de Castro, a Franciscan, writes in his book on heresies under the heading Liberty: 'There is yet another freedom, opposed to necessity, or more accurately to compulsion.' He adds that when we call man's choice free, it is this freedom that is meant.

Joseph Angles, another Franciscan and bishop-designate of Bosa, later took over Alfonso's words as his own in his commentary on the second book of the Sentences. Having spoken of the freedom of grace and the freedom of glory, he says: 'Third, there is the freedom opposed to necessity, or more accurately to compulsion. This is the freedom of nature, which is our present subject.'

Later, after distinguishing freedom from compulsion, from sin, and from misery, he concludes: 'As regards freedom in the first sense, free choice exists equally in men and in angels. The reason is that the will of neither bad nor good angels, nor of bad men, can be forced.'

Further on he asks whether the act of free choice concerns only contingent things or necessary things as well. Following Bonaventure, he notes that free choice may be viewed either as free or as deliberating, and he draws two conclusions.

First: 'The act of free choice can concern and does concern necessary things. For there is free choice in God, in the angels, and in the blessed, and it issues in its act unchangeably and necessarily, since God is unchangeable by nature and angels and the blessed by glory.'

Second: 'If free choice is taken in the second sense, its act concerns contingent things. For we do not deliberate or take counsel about what is necessary or impossible, but about contingent things that it is in our power to do or leave undone.' (On distinctions 24 and 25, the single question on free choice, arts. 1-3.)
